passage:
I sit next to Pema at the design studio, so I saw the whole thing on Thursday.
A video was flying around every group: a bridge collapsing, cars sliding into a river, with the caption "Our Ring Road flyover, just now!!" Three people in our office had already shared it. Someone was crying in the pantry.
Pema didn't share it. She paused it, zoomed in, and said, "Those cars are driving on the left, but look at the signs." Then she dragged a frame into an image search. I watched the results load. The same video, from another country, four years ago.
She checked two local news sites next. Nothing about the flyover. She called the office manager to tell the person in the pantry.
I don't know what she was feeling. She looked calm, maybe a little tired. When I asked, she just said, "If I can't find where it came from, I don't send it."
Rashmi

qa.q: How many people in the office had already shared the video?
qa.a: Three people in the office had already shared it.

qa.q: What might Pema have been thinking when she paused the video?
qa.a: Pema probably doubted the caption because details like the road signs did not fit, although Rashmi admits not knowing exactly what she felt.

qa.q: Which of Pema's steps could anyone copy before sharing?
qa.a: Looking at odd details, searching a frame to find where the video first appeared, and checking whether trusted local news carries the story.

qa.q: How was the person crying in the pantry affected by the fake?
qa.a: That person was frightened by a disaster that had not happened here, and Pema's call to the office manager was a way to calm that fear.

grounding: Rashmi watches Pema check a viral disaster video by searching for its source and trusted outlets, and refuse to share what she cannot verify.

passage:
Monday. A screenshot arrived in Imran's alumni group: a news headline saying his old company was shutting its Chennai office, with a logo that looked right. Shankar had already added, "Told you!!" Imran's thumb hovered over forward to his friends still working there. He stopped. No link, just a picture of a headline.
Wednesday. He searched the exact headline. No news site had it. On the company's own press page, the latest note was about a new Chennai hiring drive. He looked at the screenshot again: the font of the date didn't match the rest.
Friday. The fake had reached forty groups. Shankar messaged him privately. "Did you check that thing? My cousin there was panicking."
"I did. It's not real. There's no source anywhere, and the company says the opposite."
"Should've asked you first."
"Next time just don't send it until someone finds the source."

qa.q: What was the latest note on the company's press page about?
qa.a: The latest note was about a new Chennai hiring drive.

qa.q: What does Imran's hovering thumb on Monday suggest Imran was feeling?
qa.a: His thumb hovered over forward and then he stopped, which shows he doubted a headline that came only as a picture with no link.

qa.q: Which checks did Imran do before deciding the story was fake?
qa.a: He searched the exact headline on news sites, checked the company's own press page, and noticed the date font did not match.

qa.q: How has Shankar's view changed by Friday?
qa.a: Shankar is worried because a cousin at the company panicked, and now wishes Imran had been asked first instead of adding "Told you!!".

grounding: Over a week, Imran looks for the original source of a viral headline, checks trusted outlets and odd details, and does not share it.
